Resistivities at 20 degrees C from the table: aluminium 2.7 x 10^-8, iron 9.8 x 10^-8, copper 1.7 x 10^-8, fresh water 10 to 100, and a typical insulator 10^10 to 10^16 ohm-metres - about twenty-four orders of magnitude between a good conductor and an insulator.

Calculation: R = 2.7 x 10^-8 ohm-metre x 100,000 m / (300 x 10^-6 m2) = 2.7 x 10^-3 / 3 x 10^-4 = 9 ohms for the 100 km aluminium line.

Material choice: copper has a roughly 37 % lower resistivity than aluminium, so for the same resistance a copper conductor may be about a third thinner. But copper has roughly three times the density and is several times more expensive, so the copper conductor would still be about twice as heavy and far more costly - and on an overhead line the conductor weight determines the tower spacing and the tower design. Aluminium (in practice aluminium-steel composite conductors, where the steel core carries the mechanical load) is therefore the standard for overhead lines, while copper is used where the cross-section rather than the weight is the binding constraint, e.g. in cables and in windings. Iron would be unsuitable in any case: its resistivity is 3.6 times that of aluminium.

prompt: A power plant delivers 100 MW of power at a voltage of 20 kV; the line resistance is 3 ohms. State the three laws given on the slide and calculate the transmission loss for the 20 kV line, expressing the result also as a share of the transmitted power.
solution:
The three laws on the slide: (I) power P = U x I; (II) resistance R = U / I, i.e. U = R x I (Ohm's law); inserting II into I gives the line loss Pv = R x I squared. Note that the lecture works with the single-phase relation P = U x I.

Step 1 - current: I = P / U = 100 x 10^6 W / (20 x 10^3 V) = 5000 A.

Step 2 - loss: Pv = I squared x R = (5000 A) squared x 3 ohms = 25 x 10^6 x 3 = 7.5 x 10^7 W = 75 MW.

That is 75 % of the 100 MW fed into the line - three quarters of the energy would be turned into heat and the line would be unusable. The example is deliberately extreme, but the message is correct and general: the loss is driven by the current, and it grows with the square of the current. Doubling the transmitted power at the same voltage quadruples the loss.

The consequence, worked out on the following slide, is to transmit the same power at a higher voltage, because a higher voltage means a proportionally smaller current for the same power.

prompt: Same task, now for the 380 kV line (100 MW, 3 ohms): calculate the loss, compare it with the 20 kV case, derive the general relation between loss, power, resistance and voltage, and state the conclusion the slide draws.
solution:
Current: I = P / U = 100 x 10^6 W / (380 x 10^3 V) = 263 A.
Loss: Pv = I squared x R = (263 A) squared x 3 ohms = 2.1 x 10^5 W = 0.21 MW, i.e. 0.21 % of the transmitted power - against 75 MW or 75 % on the 20 kV line.

General relation: substituting I = P/U into Pv = R x I squared gives Pv = R x P squared / U squared. At constant transmitted power the loss falls with the square of the voltage and grows with the square of the power. The factor between the two cases is (380/20) squared = 361, and indeed 75 MW / 361 = 0.21 MW.

Conclusion of the slide: lower resistance, reduce current, increase voltage (transform). Of the three levers the voltage is by far the most effective, because it enters quadratically while the resistance enters only linearly - doubling the conductor cross-section halves the loss, whereas raising the voltage by a factor of 19 cuts it by a factor of 361. This is why long-distance transmission uses the extra-high-voltage levels 220 kV and 380 kV, why every step between voltage levels requires a transformer, and why low voltage is only used over the last few hundred metres to the customer.

Methodological note: the lecture uses the single-phase relation P = U x I. With the correct three-phase relation I = P / (root 3 x U x cos phi) and Pv = 3 x I squared x R the same expression Pv = R x P squared / U squared results, so the numbers are unaffected - but write down the formula the lecture uses.
